Abstract
34
Recent progress in deep learning has improved fault diagnosis, but such 
35
models typically demand large, labeled data and struggle with overfitting 
36
when data is limited or imbalanced. Collecting data under faulty machine 
37
conditions is challenging, as artificially inducing faults can damage other 
38
parts.  Additionally, feature extraction pipelines often produce high-
39
dimensional, redundant representations that hinder interpretability and 
40
efficiency. To overcome these challenges, this paper introduces a sensor-
41
fused and data-efficient framework for centrifugal pump fault diagnosis 
42
under varying pressure conditions. The proposed method uses an 
43
autoregressive (AR) observer to model normal-class signals across multiple 
44
sensors and extract residuals indicative of faults. These residuals are further 
45
processed to compute statistical and spectral descriptors such as RMS and 
46
band power. To remove irrelevant features and reduce dimensionality, an 
47
Auto-Permutation Feature Importance mechanism (Auto-PFI) is used, 
48
yielding a compact and discriminative feature set. Gaussian Mixture Model 
49
(GMM) is then trained for class-wise density estimation and fault 
50
classification. The framework is validated on datasets acquired at 3, 3.5, and 
51
4 bar pressure levels achieving accuracies of above 99% across all pressures, 
52
and its performance is benchmarked against single-sensor setups and state-
53
of-the-art method. Visualization tools including t-SNE, ROC curves, and 
54
confusion matrices confirm the robustness and generalization of the 
55
approach. Results demonstrate that integrating AR-based residual modeling 
56
with Auto-PFI and GMM classification offers a reliable, interpretable, and 
57
low-data-demanding solution for centrifugal pumps fault diagnosis.
58

1. Introduction 
62
Multistage centrifugal pumps (MCPs) are widely used in industries to convert 
63
electrical energy into mechanical energy through multiple impellers that 
64
move fluid efficiently. These pumps are a key component of industries like oil 
65
refining, mining, and power generation [1]. Because of their widespread use, 
66
any fault in MCPs can lead to energy loss, production delays, high repair costs, 
67
and even safety hazards. A recent survey showed that spending just 10,000 -
68
20,000 USD on health monitoring could save up to 500,000 USD annually, 
69
highlighting the importance of timely maintenance [2]. This makes early and 
70
accurate fault diagnosis a top priority for centrifugal pump systems.
71
Faults in MCPs can generally be divided into two categories: mechanical 
72
faults (MFs) and fluid flow-related issues [3]. Although these may be

73
interconnected, mechanical faults tend to occur more often. Among them, 
74
around 34% are related to the mechanical seal (MS), which serves as a critical 
75
component in ensuring fluid containment and shaft alignment. Besides MS 
76
faults, impeller defects are also common, and both types of faults may affect 
77
the pump's performance or fluid flow dynamics [4]. These faults can appear 
78
as hard faults, which are obvious and easy to detect, or soft faults, which 
79
gradually deteriorate pump performance without immediate functional 
80
failure. Detecting soft faults at an early stage is especially important to 
81
reduce long-term damage and associated costs.
82
Soft defects caused by a faulty MS may include fluid leakage, fretting, and 
83
shaft wear, while impeller issues can disrupt fluid dynamics and introduce 
84
mechanical instability [5,6]. To address these minute conditions effectively, 
85
this study focuses on detecting early-stage soft faults, particularly those 
86
caused by mechanical seal holes (MSH), mechanical seal scratches (MSS), 
87
and impeller defects.
88
One of the most effective tools for monitoring MCP conditions is the analysis 
89
of vibration signals. Faults introduce abrupt changes in mechanical stiffness, 
90
which in turn generate impulsive and non-stationary vibration responses[7]. 
91
These changes often appear in the frequency domain but are masked by noise 
92
due to their low energy levels [8]. Furthermore, the vibration signals from 
93
faulty machines show time-varying statistical behavior, making them non-
94
stationary and harder to interpret [9]. Standard Fourier transforms work well 
95
for stationary signals but struggle in such cases.
96
To improve signal clarity, methods like blind source separation (BSS) have 
97
been used, but they require reference signals and have limited flexibility in 
98
real-world scenarios [10]. Time-frequency representations such as the short-
99
time Fourier transform (STFT) and wavelet transform have shown better 
100
performance in analyzing non-stationary signals [11,12]. However, STFT 
101
faces a trade-off between time and frequency resolution due to its fixed 
102
window size [13,14]. Wavelet transforms offer better adaptability to non-
103
stationary impulses and have been widely used to preprocess MCP vibration 
104
signals and extract relevant features [15–17]. Nevertheless, wavelet-based 
105
methods are sensitive to the choice of mother wavelet and can introduce 
106
artifacts. Empirical mode decomposition has been proposed as an adaptive 
107
alternative but is prone to mode mixing and interpolation errors [18]. S-
108
transform has also emerged as a solution to combine the strengths of both 
109
WT and STFT [19].
110
Wavelet coherence analysis is another advanced technique that helps detect 
111
frequency-locked signals related to faults by generating coherograms, often 
112
followed by deep learning for classification [20]. Accurate classification 
113
depends not only on preprocessing but also on effective feature extraction. 
114
Discriminative features from time, frequency, and time–frequency domains 
115
must be carefully selected to reflect the nature of faults [21,22]. Deep

116
learning methods have gained attention for automating feature extraction 
117
and classification [23–26] and have shown promising results in fault diagnosis 
118
for centrifugal pumps [27]. However, soft faults in MCPs introduce additional 
119
complexity due to fluid structure interaction. Traditional features extracted 
120
from raw signals often fail to capture these interactions, especially when 
121
signal quality is poor or when operating under low-pressure conditions. Time-
122
domain features may not be sensitive enough to detect early-stage faults, and 
123
frequency-domain features are often blocked by noise from microstructural 
124
vibrations. Another issue is that most of the deep learning models require 
125
many samples for a better generalization and reliable performance. Another 
126
problem is that all the features extracted are not necessary to be beneficial 
127
for the study. Past studies have also explored feature selection and 
128
dimensionality reduction using methods like Principal Component Analysis 
129
(PCA) and Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) [28,29]. While PCA captures 
130
overall signal variations, it fails to account for class separability. LDA 
131
improves on this but still requires large, labeled datasets and faces 
132
challenges in optimizing intraclass discrimination [30]. Furthermore, recent 
133
studies also show that fault diagnosis becomes more challenging when 
134
operating conditions vary across domains. Jian et al. [31] proposed an 
135
imbalance-aware prototype-guided contrastive learning framework that 
136
demonstrated how distribution drift and underrepresented fault classes 
137
degrade performance across changing operating states. Related work on 
138
open-set domain generalization introduced dual-level weighted mechanisms 
139
and targeted data augmentation to cope with unknown or unmatched 
140
operating domains, highlighting that fault features often shift when 
141
conditions change [32]. A two-stage semi-supervised domain generalization 
142
approach further combining imbalance correction with domain-invariant 
143
feature extraction to manage label scarcity and cross-domain drift 
144
simultaneously [33]. In addition, long-tailed multi-domain generalization has 
145
been explored using moment-matching and balanced contrastive strategies 
146
to stabilize feature distributions under unequal class frequencies and 
147
variable conditions [34]. In addition, Zhang et al. [35] proposed a 
148
generalizable diagnosis framework based on synthetic and adversarial 
149
sample learning, where a modified 1-D diffusion model generates samples for 
150
unseen working states and adversarial samples are injected using fast-
151
gradient perturbations to enhance robustness against distribution shifts. This 
152
approach significantly improves performance in gearbox diagnostics under 
153
unseen operating conditions. Complementary to this, Han et al. [36] 
154
introduced a health-aware joint scale-distribution learning strategy for 
155
unsupervised anomaly detection, where intrinsic EL-image patterns are 
156
modeled through scale learning and compact embeddings are constructed to 
157
improve discriminability under contaminated or nonstationary data 
158
scenarios.Beyond these domain-centric methods, Siddique et al. [37] 
159
introduced a semi-supervised Vision Transformer framework that leverages 
160
pseudo-label generation, uncertainty-aware refinement, and teacher–student

161
knowledge distillation to enhance robustness when labeled samples are 
162
limited. Although the model achieved high accuracy across milling cutting 
163
tool datasets, its reliance on iterative pseudo-label refinement and 
164
transformer-based architecture requires substantial computational resources 
165
and large-scale unlabeled data. Collectively, these studies confirm that 
166
distribution shift, class imbalance, and domain variability significantly affect 
167
diagnostic performance under varying operating conditions, while most state-
168
of-the-art methods depend on deep multi-stage architectures that demand 
169
extensive training effort and sizable datasets.
170
To overcome these issues, this paper introduces a residual-based 
171
preprocessing framework that models the normal behavior of MCPs using an 
172
autoregressive (AR) observer. This observer captures the expected response 
173
of the system under healthy conditions, and any deviation (residual) 
174
highlights possible faults. By extracting residuals from multiple sensors, we 
175
amplify the fault signatures while suppressing background interference. 
176
These residuals are then processed to extract statistical features across time 
177
and frequency domain. Rather than relying on manual selection, we use an 
178
automated permutation feature importance (Auto-PFI) strategy to identify the 
179
most informative features. This ensures interpretability and avoids overfitting. 
180
For final classification, a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) is utilized to model 
181
the probability distributions of different fault types. GMMs are well-suited for 
182
noisy, low-sample scenarios and provide soft decision outputs based on 
183
likelihood scores. The proposed residual-based learning pipeline further 
184
addresses the challenges of variable operating pressures, class imbalance, 
185
and redundant high-dimensional representations by generating pressure-
186
robust residuals and selecting only the most discriminative features for 
187
reliable fault discrimination. The novelty and main contributions of this study 
188
are given below:
189
1) A residual-centric autoregressive (AR) observer trained under normal 
190
pressure conditions is developed to generate deviation residuals that 
191
selectively highlight fault-related disturbances while suppressing 
192
periodic flow and operational noise. This residual formulation enhances 
193
the visibility of early-stage soft faults such as MSH, MSS, and impeller 
194
degradation.
195
2) Multi-sensor residual fusion is introduced to capture complementary 
196
fault characteristics from three vibration sensors positioned at different 
197
structural locations. This fusion strategy provides a more stable and 
198
discriminative 
representation 
than 
single-sensor 
approaches, 
199
particularly in complex MCP geometries where fault signatures 
200
propagate unevenly.
201
3) A hybrid residual-feature extraction pipeline combined with an Auto-
202
PFI selection mechanism identifies the most pressure-invariant and 
203
discriminative features across time, frequency, and statistical domains. 
204
Auto-PFI removes redundant or noise-sensitive features, ensuring

compactness and preventing overfitting under variable operating

conditions.
207
4) A structured residual-feature space is modeled using a Gaussian

216

2. Experimental Setup 
219
To facilitate fault diagnosis experiments, a dedicated test environment was 
220
established featuring a PMT-4008 MCP (manufactured by Hanil, Gwangju, 
221
Republic of Korea), operated by a 5.5 kW electric motor. The system was 
222
equipped with a comprehensive control interface that allowed fine control 
223
over key parameters such as temperature, flow rate, speed, and power, along 
224
with a visual display and multiple operational switches. The pump system was 
225
integrated with two vertically elevated water storage units; a main tank and 
226
a buffer tank to guarantee a net positive suction head (NPSH) at the pump’s 
227
inlet. These tanks ensured stable water flow and minimized cavitation risk. 
228
The hydraulic circuit connecting the pump and tanks utilized steel pipelines 
229
fitted with pressure gauges and manual valves, ensuring accurate monitoring 
230
and safe flow regulation throughout the test duration. Figure 1 shows the real 
231
time picture of the experimental set up whereas Figure 2 shows the 
232
schematics of this experimental setup.

2.1 Sensor Placement 
238
To capture high-fidelity vibration signals from the MCP, three PCB 622B01 
239
piezoelectric accelerometers were strategically affixed to the pump casing 
240
and key internal components. These sensors were mounted closer to the 
241
pump casing and positioned near the impeller and mechanical seal region. All 
242
sensors were secured with adhesive to ensure stability during operation at 
243
1733 rpm.
244
The sensors operated with a sensitivity of 100 mV/g + 5% and supported a 
245
frequency bandwidth of 0.42 - 10 kHz, effectively covering the expected 
246
vibration spectrum. Their analog signals were digitized using a National 
247
Instruments NI-9234 data acquisition module, which offered 24-bit ADC 
248
resolution across four analog input channels, capable of handling input 
249
signals up to 13.1 MHz.
250
2.2 Fault Conditions
251
To generate training data for fault classification, the following faults were 
252
artificially introduced into the system using controlled modifications:
253
a. Mechanical Seal Hole 
254
Two mechanical seals with 38 mm inner diameter were used. For the MSH 
255
condition, a 2.8 mm diameter and 2.8 mm depth hole was drilled into the 
256
rotating component of the seal. The stationary component remained 
257
untouched to isolate the faulty source.

b. Mechanical Seal Scratch

For the MSS fault, a deliberate scratch of 10 mm length, 2.5 mm diameter,

c. Impeller Corrosion
263
To replicate impeller corrosion, a region of metal was removed from a cast-

defect was 18 mm long, 2.5 mm wide, and 2.8 mm deep, inscribed within a 
266
broader impeller diameter of 161 mm.
267
These fault conditions were selected to reflect real-world deterioration

mechanisms in industrial pumping systems and were carefully designed to

preserve the structural integrity of surrounding components, allowing clean

and isolated signal capture from each fault type. Figure 3 shows the pictures

3. Proposed Method
276
The proposed fault diagnosis framework for MCP comprises six primary 
277
stages, as illustrated in Figure 4. First, vibration signals are acquired from 
278
MCPs under multiple fault types and pressure levels. An AR observer, trained 
279
on normal signals, models healthy behavior and generates residuals by 
280
subtracting predicted outputs from actual signals. From these residuals, a 
281
rich set of features is extracted, pruned through correlation analysis, and 
282
ranked using PFI. Finally, a GMM classifies faults based on the selected 
283
features, using probabilistic inference to handle class overlaps and severity 
284
variations. Each stage is described step by step below:

3.5
Multi-Sensor Feature Fusion Under Variable Pressures
435
In this work, the three vibration sensors are first processed independently to 
436
preserve their individual sensitivity to fault-related dynamics. Each sensor 
437
signal is modeled using the autoregressive observer to generate a residual 
438
sequence that highlights deviations from normal behavior. Treating sensors 
439
separately prevents interference arising from differences in amplitude 
440
scaling, phase response, and pressure-dependent vibration characteristics 
441
across 3, 3.5, and 4 bar conditions. Statistical and frequency-domain features 
442
are then extracted from each sensor’s residuals, ensuring that local and 
443
global information related to pump faults is retained.
444
Feature-level fusion is performed by concatenating the three sensor feature 
445
vectors into a unified representation. This late fusion approach is preferred 
446
over early fusion because operating pressure variations affect each sensor 
447
differently and combining raw or residual signals directly tends to amplify 
448
distribution drift. By fusing features after residual generation, the model 
449
works with normalized, pressure-robust descriptors. The Auto-PFI module 
450
then filters the fused set, removing redundant or pressure-sensitive features 
451
and retaining the most discriminative ones for downstream classification.

460

464

466

Results and Discussion 
495
The proposed framework introduces a sensor-fused and data-efficient 
496
approach for centrifugal pump fault diagnosis under varying pressure 
497
conditions. By using an AR observer to extract residuals across three sensors 
498
and refining these through Auto-PFI before classification with GMM, the 
499
method achieves high discriminability while maintaining interpretability. To 
500
further assess the advantage of using multi-sensors, an ablation study is 
501
conducted where the same framework was trained using data from only one 
502
sensor (Sensor 1, Sensor 2, or Sensor 3). This isolates the effect of sensor 
503
fusion, demonstrating the performance trade-offs when discarding multi-
504
sensor integration. Furthermore, another ablation study is performed 
505
highlighting the effectiveness of the Auto-PFI in the proposed method.
506
For comparison, a state-of-the-art method is used that adapts the Multiscale 
507
Permutation Entropy with Local Linear Tangent Space Alignment (MPE-
508
LLTSA) approach. The method captures nonlinear dynamics and embeds 
509
signals into a tangent space for fault discrimination [38]. However, its 
510
dependence on handcrafted entropy features and dimensionality reduction 
511
introduces sensitivity to noise and pressure variations, which may limit its 
512
discriminative power in complex fault scenarios.
513
The method is also compared with Swarm Intelligence Optimization Entropy 
514
(SIOE) based model with XGBoost classification. Here, entropy parameters 
515
are optimized using African Vulture Optimization and logistic chaos theory, 
516
enabling adaptive feature extraction [39]. XGBoost then performs 
517
classification by using robust ensemble learning. While this method improves 
518
entropy-based fault detection and demonstrates higher adaptability than 
519
static entropy measures, it remains constrained by entropy’s sensitivity to 
520
local variations and lacks the residual-modeling capability of the proposed 
521
approach.
522
The method is further compared with a recently proposed Multi-scale Hybrid 
523
Domain Adaptation with Attention (MHD AA) network, which combines multi-
524
scale convolutional feature extractors with a multi-channel attention 
525
mechanism to capture fault-related structures from different receptive fields 
526
[40]. The network also incorporates a hybrid domain adaptation strategy to 
527
align distributions between source and target domains, making it suitable for 
528
unsupervised rotating machinery diagnosis under varying operating 
529
conditions. When applied to the centrifugal pump dataset, the model 
530
produces the performance values shown in Table 3 and the feature 
531
distribution trends illustrated in Figure 15, where the t-SNE visualization 
532
exhibits partial clustering but still reveals noticeable overlap between MSH 
533
and MSS samples. While the multi-scale and attention components enrich 
534
local feature representation, the reliance on domain adaptation alignment 
535
limits its ability to fully discriminate highly similar mechanical seal faults, 
536
especially when noise and pressure variations distort the underlying feature

552
Since the DEF model depends on handcrafted feature groups and lacks 
553
residual-based modeling, its robustness decreases when fault signatures 
554
become highly similar or distorted by load fluctuations. 
555
To evaluate the diagnostic performance of the proposed framework, four 
556
commonly used metrics are employed: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-
557
score. Accuracy measures the proportion of correctly classified samples but 
558
may become misleading when the dataset is imbalanced because it is 
559
dominated by majority classes. Precision quantifies how many of the 
560
predicted fault samples are truly correct, which is important for avoiding 
561
false alarms in industrial monitoring. Recall measures the proportion of 
562
correctly detected fault samples relative to the total actual samples of that 
563
class, making it critical for identifying weak or early-stage faults. The F1-
564
score, defined as the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall, provides a 
565
balanced assessment when class distributions are uneven [42]. Table 3 
566
summarizes the performance across all methods. The proposed framework 
567
consistently performed better as compared to both ablation and comparison 
568
models, achieving accuracies of 99.64%, 99.29%, and 99.67% at 3, 3.5, and 
569
4 bar pressures, respectively. Precision, recall, and F1-scores remained 
570
above 99.2% across all operating conditions, confirming robustness to 
571
pressure variations. By contrast, the ablation study results dropped to 96.40% 
572
(Sensor 1), 97.84% (Sensor 2), and 96.04% (Sensor 3). This indicates that 
573
while individual sensors contribute useful information, fusion markedly 
574
improves reliability. Sensor 2 provided slightly stronger results among the 
575
single-sensor setups, but none matched the fused configuration. When the 
576
proposed method was used without using Auto-PFI, although utilizing all the 
577
three sensors, the method achieved an accuracy of 96.04%, precision 96.68%, 
578
recall and F1 score 95.58% and 96% respectively.

626
First, autoregressive residual modeling captures deviations from normal 
627
behavior, providing fault-indicative features that entropy-based methods 
628

629
features, ensuring compact yet highly discriminative input for classification.

Conclusion and Future Recommendations
637
This study proposed a sensor-fused framework for MCPs fault diagnosis 
638
under varying pressure conditions. By integrating AR residual modeling, 
639
Auto-PFI, and GMM based classification, the method achieved better 
640
performance, with accuracy exceeding 99% across 3, 3.5, and 4 bar datasets. 
641
The ablation study confirmed that multi-sensor fusion performs better than 
642
the single-sensor setups, while comparative analysis against state-of-the-art 
643
entropy-based methods further highlighted the robustness of the proposed 
644
approach. Visualization through confusion matrices, t-SNE, and ROC curves 
645
validated the robustness, separability, and generalization capability of the 
646
framework.
647
The key advantage lies in combining residual-driven fault indicators with 
648
adaptive feature selection and sensor fusion, which collectively enhance 
649
discriminative power and resilience to operating variations. These 
650
contributions establish the framework as a reliable and interpretable solution 
651
for intelligent condition monitoring of centrifugal pumps. In future work, the 
652
framework can be extended to other rotating machinery and real-time 
653
monitoring scenarios and can be further strengthened by incorporating 
654
noise-perturbation 
robustness 
tests, 
unseen-condition 
generalization 
655
experiments, and extended perturbation studies, with potential integration 
656
into industrial digital twin platforms for predictive maintenance.

Abstract: 34 Recent progress in deep learning has improved fault diagnosis, but such 35 models typically demand large, labeled data and struggle with overfitting 36 when data is limited or imbalanced. Collecting data under faulty machine 37 conditions is challenging, as artificially inducing faults can damage other 38 parts. Additionally, feature extraction pipelines often produce high- 39 dimensional, redundant representations that hinder interpretability and 40 efficiency. To overcome these challenges, this paper introduces a sensor- 41 fused and data-efficient framework for centrifugal pump fault diagnosis 42 under varying pressure conditions. The proposed method uses an 43 autoregressive (AR) observer to model normal-class signals across multiple 44 sensors and extract residuals indicative of faults. These residuals are further 45 processed to compute statistical and spectral descriptors such as RMS and 46 band power. To remove irrelevant features and reduce dimensionality, an 47 Auto-Permutation Feature Importance mechanism (Auto-PFI) is used, 48 yielding a compact and discriminative feature set. Gaussian Mixture Model 49 (GMM) is then trained for class-wise density estimation and fault 50 classification. The framework is validated on datasets acquired at 3, 3.5, and 51 4 bar pressure levels achieving accuracies of above 99% across all pressures, 52 and its performance is benchmarked against single-sensor setups and state- 53 of-the-art method. Visualization tools including t-SNE, ROC curves, and 54 confusion matrices confirm the robustness and generalization of the 55 approach. Results demonstrate that integrating AR-based residual modeling 56 with Auto-PFI and GMM classification offers a reliable, interpretable, and 57 low-data-demanding solution for centrifugal pumps fault diagnosis. 58
